pattern_stance_changes.reason: 'Mixed' needs an isolating comparison with a split result, and the paper has none. The C4 figures (8.4% breaking explicit constraints such as .cursorignore, 7.1% unauthorized command execution, 2.0% ignored permission-required settings) are shares of complaint posts, and the only author check is one reproduction of Copilot reading .env after two debugging prompts (§1, Fig. 1). No condition enforces policy while another does not, and nothing is measured outside the agent loop. The authors propose strict defaults, sensitive-file protection and enforcement of developer-specified access controls (§5) without testing them, which is 'introduces'. The bypass reports matter as existence evidence that in-host ignore files and allowlists are not a security boundary; that belongs in the contribution, not the stance.

The paper goes beyond mentioning approval gates. §5 argues that auto-apply features 'circumvent manual scrutiny' and calls for developer-in-the-loop mitigation, and the closing message to users (§8) is to 'verify LIDE-suggested code changes before approval'. That is a recommendation with no comparison, so 'introduces' rather than 'neutral'.

missed_issues: The false-negative audit cannot support the claim that 'residual false-negative risk after LLM filtering is low' (§2.2). The filter was checked on 100 plus 200 LLM-negative posts, with 0 misses. Relevant posts make up roughly 0.04% of even the smallest corpus size the paper gives (446 of 1.1M posts). At that base rate, a 300-post negative sample would be expected to contain about 0.1 relevant posts even if recall were 50%, so it cannot tell 50% recall from 100%. The rule-of-three bound (3/300 = 1% of negatives) allows thousands of missed posts. The taxonomy may therefore be incomplete in favour of issue types the 20-post seed prompt recognises.

No inter-rater agreement is reported for the issue coding that produces the 32 issues and every category percentage. The kappa of 0.967 covers only binary relevance screening (§2.2, Table 2), and the kappa of 0.99 covers only mitigation labels (§2.3). Issue codes were assigned by two authors and finalised by consensus (§2.3). The review's claim-1 evidence cites the relevance kappa without noting that the taxonomy itself is unmeasured.

P22 is not tagged. Prompt injection is 2.7% of security posts (§3.2, e.g. a malicious prompt merged into Amazon Q through a pull request), and MCP tool-poisoning reports also appear (§3.2). The paper tests no defence, so the stance would be 'neutral' at most.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats, COI none, the review's weak and unsupported claim grades (including the 1.1M/29-subreddit figure that the methods never derive), and its neutral stances on P20, P09, P01 and P04. My scores differ by one point on three axes. Rigor is 2 against the review's 3, because the recall audit has no power at this base rate and the taxonomy coding has no reliability measure; the merge takes 2. Generalizability is 2 against 3 (Reddit only, self-selected incidents). Relevance is 3 against 2: the paper bears directly on where a harness enforces deny rules and keeps secrets, and the merge takes 2. I move P21 from mixed to introduces because there is no isolating comparison, only bypass reports, and P19 from neutral to introduces because the authors recommend verification before approval. The reproduced Copilot .env read is the single author-confirmed incident, and it is the strongest reason not to treat host ignore files as a boundary.
